bib.title: Compositional Skill Routing for LLM Agents: Decompose, Retrieve, and Compose

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 14 of 14 pages (53,679 chars), including limitations and Appendices A-L. Extraction was clean. No embedded instructions.

SOURCE: "Compositional Skill Routing for LLM Agents: Decompose, Retrieve, and Compose", Xueping Gao, Alibaba Cloud (Hangzhou). Single author. arXiv 2606.18051v1 [cs.CL], 16 Jun 2026. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

CORE CLAIM: Skill routing is usually single-skill selection, but real queries need several skills. The paper proposes SKILLWEAVER (LLM decomposer, MiniLM bi-encoder with FAISS, DAG composer) and the COMPSKILLBENCH benchmark. It finds that decomposition granularity (getting the right number of sub-tasks) is the bottleneck. Its fix is SAD: retrieve skills for the first-pass sub-tasks, then re-decompose with the retrieved skill names as hints.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (all on COMPSKILLBENCH: 300 synthetic template queries, 2,209 real awesome-mcp-servers entries, 24 categories; decomposer Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, T=0.1; all-MiniLM-L6-v2; V100; H=15 hints; one run, no seeds reported)
- Decomposition accuracy (DA, exact step count) goes from 51.0% to 67.7% with SAD (Wilcoxon p<1e-6, n=300; bootstrap CI on the DA gain [+10.3, +23.0] pp). DA±1 goes from 71.3% to 84.3%.
- Category recall at 1 (CatR@1) goes from 34.2% to 37.0%. This is NOT significant (p=0.17). CatR@10 is about 69-70%.
- Context cost (Table 3): exposing all 2,209 skills is about 884K tokens, assuming about 400 tokens per skill (an estimate, not measured). Top-10 retrieval is about 4,000 tokens (99.5% reduction). SKILLWEAVER at 2.9 skills per query is about 1,160 tokens (99.9%). SAD pass 2 adds a fixed ~1,100 tokens of hints.
- Listing skills in the prompt (LLM-Direct): qwen-max shown 100 skill names that include the ground truth gets DA 0.90 but CatR@1 only 0.211. n=50.
- A ReAct-style qwen-max agent gets DA 0 (the paper says this is a protocol mismatch).
- Cross-model, n=50 each: Qwen2.5-14B DA goes 32% to 68%. qwen-max DA goes 66% to 92%.
- Pilot execution with mock executors: 76.7% chain completion (23/30), 86.9% step success.

ABLATIONS
- Oracle step count: a vanilla 7B told the true K reaches DA 99.3% and CatR@1 39.8%. SAD's DA=1-conditioned figure is 41.2%. So SAD works mainly as a granularity corrector.
- On the 128 queries where both methods get DA right, CatR@1 is identical (41.7% vs 40.9%, p=0.97).
- SAD fixes 75 queries (25%). On those, CatR@1 goes from 23.6% to 37.0%.
- Hint count H=5/10/15/25 gives DA 0.550/0.597/0.677/0.687.
- Rounds: DA is flat after round 1. CatR@1 peaks at round 2 (0.389) and falls at round 3 (0.361).
- Listwise reranker pilot (same 7B, no training): CatR@1 goes from 0.371 to 0.409 (+3.8 pp, p=0.007). 53 queries improved and 25 got worse. It adds about 1.4 s per sub-task, and per-query latency is about 5 s.
- BGE-base encoder, n=50: CatR@1 goes from 0.394 to 0.451.
- Transfer (Table 5): relative DA gain is +35.6% with 2 categories held out (n=62) and +23.2% with 20% of skills held out (n=100).
- Human-style queries (n=200): strict DA goes from 8.5% to 21.5%, DA±1 from 30.5% to 50.5%.

QUOTES
- p.2: "Standard LLM decomposition achieves only 34.2% CatR@1 on a pool of 2,209 real skills."
- p.6 (§7.3): "listing skills in the prompt is insufficient—even a much stronger model cannot match retrieval-based routing with SAD"
- p.6: "SAD's CatR@1 gain comes entirely from unlocking correct retrieval via granularity correction, not from vocabulary alignment per se."
- p.9 (Limitations): "Our evaluation is retrieval-focused; we measure whether the correct skill category is retrieved, not whether the exact skill is selected or successfully executed."

LIMITS
- The queries are synthetic, built from template verb phrases. Only the skill pool is real.
- The metric is category recall, not exact skill and not execution.
- The compose stage (Eq. 4) is never evaluated on its own.
- The execution pilot uses mock executors with success rates of 80-95%.
- The 7B decomposer dominates the results. Only qwen-max and 14B were spot-checked, on 50 queries each. GPT-4o and Claude were not tested.
- The headline "+32.7%" is relative, not points. The absolute gain is 16.7 pp.
- The CatR@1 gain is not significant in aggregate.
- Skills here are MCP server descriptions, not SKILL.md bodies. Body-aware encoding is described in Eq. 3, but I did not find the results comparing it with metadata-only. The "metadata suffices" claim rests on CatR@10 of 69.0%.
- The 99% context saving is an estimate (400 tokens per skill assumed), not a measured accuracy-versus-context trade-off.
- Convergence is argued by pigeonhole, which is weak.
- Single author. Preprint.

BUILDS ON: SkillRouter (Zheng et al., 2025, arXiv 2603.22455; single-skill bi-encoder). Dense Passage Retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020, EMNLP). Anthropic's SKILL.md Agent Skills spec (2025) and MCP (2024). CRAFT (Yuan et al., 2025, ICLR). MCP-Zero (Wang et al., 2025). FAISS (Johnson et al., 2019). Decomposed Prompting (Khot et al., 2023). Related: Self-RAG, ReAct, Reflexion, ToolLLM, Gorilla, AnyTool, TaskWeaver. The SAD hint-feedback idea is only loosely tied to these.

FIT: Weak-to-moderate for 03-tool-design.md. The best section is "Tool discovery at scale". It supports three points: retrieval over a large skill library cuts context by orders of magnitude; dumping 100 names into the prompt performed worse than retrieval; and decompose-then-retrieve with a hint feedback loop helps. Use it only as a single-preprint sharpens citation. It does not fit "Progressive disclosure: skills" (it never studies disclosure of SKILL.md bodies) or "Writing a skill" (it says nothing about authoring skills, except that vague descriptions lose retrieval, per the error analysis in Appendix J).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig. 1 (p.2), the decompose, retrieve, compose pipeline with the SAD feedback arrow. It is a simple diagram. Table 3 (context tokens) may be more useful than any figure.
